items.q: She ____ to work by bus every day.
items.w: Third person singular in the present simple takes -s: he/she/it goes.

items.q: Be quiet — the baby ____.
items.w: Something happening right now takes the present continuous: is + -ing.

items.q: We ____ the match last Friday.
items.w: A finished time ("last Friday") takes the past simple.

items.q: I ____ in this city since 2019.
items.w: "Since" marks something starting in the past and still true: present perfect.

items.q: ____ you ever ____ to Japan?
items.w: Life experience with no stated time takes the present perfect: have been.

items.q: I ____ dinner when the phone rang.
items.w: A longer action interrupted by a shorter one takes the past continuous.

items.q: By the time we arrived, the film ____.
items.w: The earlier of two past events takes the past perfect: had started.

items.q: Look at those clouds — it ____ rain.
items.w: Present evidence for a future event takes "going to", not "will".

items.q: By next June I ____ here for ten years.
items.w: Completed before a future point: will have + past participle.

items.q: My eyes hurt — I ____ at this screen all morning.
items.w: An action continuing up to now, with the duration in focus, takes have been + -ing.

items.q: She is ____ engineer at a shipping firm.
items.w: "An" before a vowel sound: an engineer.

items.q: ____ sun rose at six.
items.w: Unique things take "the": the sun, the moon, the earth.

items.q: I do not drink ____ coffee in the evening.
items.w: An uncountable noun in a general sense takes no article.

items.q: There is not ____ milk left.
items.w: "Much" goes with uncountable nouns; "many" with countable ones.

items.q: ____ of my friends live abroad.
items.w: "Several" takes a plural countable noun and a plural verb.

items.q: She has ____ patience for excuses.
items.w: "Little" (without "a") means almost none, and pairs with an uncountable noun.

items.q: The meeting is ____ Monday morning.
items.w: Days and dates take "on": on Monday.

items.q: We will be there ____ six o'clock.
items.w: Clock times take "at": at six o'clock.

items.q: She has worked here ____ three years.
items.w: "For" takes a length of time; "since" takes a starting point.

items.q: He is very good ____ explaining difficult ideas.
items.w: "Good at" is the fixed pairing, and a verb after a preposition takes -ing.

items.q: The decision depends ____ the budget.
items.w: "Depend" is always followed by "on".

items.q: I must apologise ____ being late.
items.w: You apologise TO a person FOR a thing.

items.q: If it ____ tomorrow, we will stay in.
items.w: First conditional: if + present simple, then will + infinitive. Never "will" in the if-clause.

items.q: If I ____ you, I would take the job.
items.w: The second conditional uses "were" for every person: if I were you.

items.q: If she ____ harder, she would have passed.
items.w: Third conditional: if + past perfect, then would have + past participle.

items.q: If I had taken that job, I ____ in Dhaka now.
items.w: A past condition with a present result: had + past participle, then would + infinitive.

items.q: You ____ smoke in the hospital.
items.w: Modals take no auxiliary and no "to": must not smoke.

items.q: You ____ be tired after that journey.
items.w: "Must" expresses a confident deduction, not only obligation.

items.q: I ____ swim when I was six.
items.w: "Could" is the past of general ability.

items.q: She ____ the email — she never received it.
items.w: "Cannot have + past participle" expresses certainty that something did NOT happen.

items.q: You ____ told me — I would have helped.
items.w: "Should have + past participle" is regret about the past.

items.q: The bridge ____ in 1890.
items.w: Passive past simple: was/were + past participle.

items.q: The results ____ tomorrow.
items.w: The results receive the action, so the passive is needed: will be announced.

items.q: She said she ____ tired.
items.w: Reported speech shifts the tense back one step: "I am" becomes "she was".

items.q: He asked me where ____.
items.w: A reported question takes statement word order and a backshifted tense.

items.q: The man ____ car was stolen called the police.
items.w: "Whose" marks possession: the man whose car.

items.q: The book, ____ I read last year, is still my favourite.
items.w: A non-defining clause after a comma takes "which", never "that".

items.q: I really enjoy ____ early.
items.w: "Enjoy" is always followed by the -ing form.

items.q: She agreed ____ the report by Friday.
items.w: "Agree" is followed by the infinitive with "to".

items.q: I stopped ____ coffee because it kept me awake.
items.w: "Stop + -ing" means you ended the habit; "stop to drink" means you paused in order to drink.

items.q: Not only ____ late, but he also forgot the tickets.
items.w: A negative adverbial at the front inverts the subject and auxiliary: was he.

items.q: This exam was ____ than the last one.
items.w: Adjectives of three or more syllables take "more", not "-er".

items.q: It is ____ film I have ever seen.
items.w: A superlative takes "the": the best.

items.q: Each of the students ____ a folder.
items.w: "Each" is singular however many follow it, so the verb is singular.

items.q: The news ____ better today.
items.w: "News" looks plural but takes a singular verb.

items.q: Neither the manager nor the staff ____ been told.
items.w: With "neither…nor", the verb agrees with the nearer subject: staff have.

items.q: She ____ goes to bed before midnight.
items.w: Adverbs of frequency go before the main verb: she never goes.

items.q: I have ____ finished the first chapter.
items.w: "Already" is used in affirmative sentences; "yet" belongs in questions and negatives.

items.q: The rain did not ____ our plans.
items.w: "Affect" is the verb; "effect" is normally the noun.

items.q: There are ____ chairs than people.
items.w: "Fewer" for countable nouns, "less" for uncountable ones.

items.q: ____ going to be a long meeting.
items.w: "It's" is "it is". "Its" without an apostrophe is the possessive.

items.q: The company laid ____ two hundred workers.
items.w: "Lay off" means to make redundant.

items.q: I am looking forward to ____ from you.
items.w: "Looking forward to" ends in a preposition, so the verb takes -ing.

items.q: The evidence ____ the theory.
items.w: "Corroborate" means to support with evidence; "collaborate" means to work together.

items.q: Water ____ at one hundred degrees Celsius.
items.w: A general fact takes the present simple, with -s after a singular subject.

items.q: My brother ____ like coffee at all.
items.w: Present simple negatives take does not after he, she or it.

items.q: ____ your parents live nearby?
items.w: "Parents" is plural, so the question takes the auxiliary "do".

items.q: She rarely ____ television during the week.
items.w: An adverb of frequency does not remove the -s ending: she watches.

items.q: Where is Mia? She ____ in the garden.
items.w: Something in progress at this moment takes is + -ing.

items.q: I ____ my keys right now — have you seen them?
items.w: A search happening at the moment of speaking takes the present continuous.

items.q: You ____ always ____ my sentences!
items.w: The present continuous with "always" complains about a repeated habit.

items.q: Do not disturb her — she ____ for tomorrow’s viva.
items.w: An activity in progress right now takes is + -ing.

items.q: She ____ born in Chattogram.
items.w: "Be born" about one person in the past takes "was".

items.q: They ____ not come to the wedding.
items.w: The past simple negative is did not followed by the base verb.

items.q: When ____ you ____ your first job?
items.w: After "did" the verb returns to its base form: did you get.

items.q: I ____ my homework before dinner yesterday.
items.w: "Yesterday" is a finished time, so the past simple is used.

items.q: She ____ just ____ the report.
items.w: "Just", with the result still standing, takes has + past participle.

items.q: I ____ never ____ such a beautiful sunset.
items.w: Life experience with "never" takes the present perfect: have seen.

items.q: We ____ known each other for twenty years.
items.w: "For" plus a period reaching the present takes have known.

items.q: ____ you finished the assignment yet?
items.w: "Yet" in a question belongs with the present perfect.

items.q: I ____ my wallet, so I cannot pay for this.
items.w: The loss still matters now, which is what the present perfect marks.

items.q: Shakespeare ____ thirty-seven plays.
items.w: A life that has ended takes the past simple, however famous the result.

items.q: I ____ him at the conference last March.
items.w: "Last March" states a finished time, which rules out the present perfect.

items.q: She ____ in three countries so far.
items.w: "So far" marks a period still running, so the present perfect is used.

items.q: What ____ you ____ at eight o’clock last night?
items.w: An action in progress at a stated past moment takes was/were + -ing.

items.q: While she ____, someone knocked at the door.
items.w: The longer background action takes the past continuous.

items.q: They ____ not ____ attention when the announcement came.
items.w: The past continuous negative is was/were not followed by -ing.

items.q: It ____ heavily all afternoon, so we called the trip off.
items.w: Conditions running through a past period take the past continuous.

items.q: She told me she ____ the email that morning.
items.w: An event earlier than the moment being reported takes the past perfect.

items.q: I did not recognise him because he ____ his beard.
items.w: The shaving came before the failure to recognise, so it takes had + participle.

items.q: After they ____ the contract, work began on site.
items.w: "After" with two past events puts the earlier one in the past perfect.

items.q: No sooner ____ she arrived than the power went out.
items.w: "No sooner … than" takes the past perfect, inverted: had she arrived.

items.q: I ____ you tomorrow, I promise.
items.w: A promise made as you speak takes "will".

items.q: We ____ dinner with the Rahmans on Friday — it is all arranged.
items.w: A fixed personal arrangement takes the present continuous.

items.q: This time next week I ____ on a beach.
items.w: An action in progress at a future moment takes will be + -ing.

items.q: She has already decided: she ____ medicine.
items.w: An intention decided before speaking takes "going to".

items.q: By the time you read this, I ____.
items.w: Finished before a future point: will have + past participle.

items.q: ____ they ____ the bridge by December?
items.w: "By December" asks about completion, which takes the future perfect.

items.q: In August we ____ married for fifty years.
items.w: A duration complete at a future point takes will have been.

items.q: I ____ the whole series by the weekend.
items.w: "By the weekend" sets a future deadline, so the future perfect is used.

items.q: She ____ for the exam since March.
items.w: An activity running from a past point up to now takes has been + -ing.

items.q: The roads are soaked — it ____.
items.w: Present evidence of an activity only just stopping takes has been + -ing.

items.q: My hands are covered in paint — I ____ the kitchen.
items.w: The focus is the activity that left the traces, not a finished result.

items.q: They ____ about the same clause all morning and still have not agreed.
items.w: An unfinished activity through a period reaching now takes have been + -ing.

items.q: If it ____ tomorrow, we will move the ceremony indoors.
items.w: The "if" half of a first conditional uses the present simple, never "will".

items.q: You will miss the bus unless you ____ now.
items.w: "Unless" behaves like "if not" and takes the present simple.

items.q: If she ____ the deadline, the client ____ the contract.
items.w: First conditional: present simple in the if-clause, will in the other.

items.q: I ____ you as soon as the results ____ out.
items.w: After "as soon as" the present simple already carries future meaning.

items.q: If I ____ you, I would take the offer.
items.w: The second conditional uses "were" for every subject: if I were you.

items.q: If we ____ more time, we ____ the whole coast.
items.w: Second conditional: past simple in the if-clause, would in the other.

items.q: She would travel more if she ____ the money.
items.w: The if-clause of a second conditional takes the past simple.

items.q: What ____ you do if the visa ____ refused?
items.w: An unlikely situation takes would in the main clause and the past in the other.

items.q: If she ____ earlier, she would have caught the train.
items.w: The third conditional uses the past perfect in the if-clause.

items.q: We ____ the flight if the road had been clear.
items.w: The main clause of a third conditional is would have + past participle.

items.q: Had I known about the strike, I ____ another route.
items.w: "Had I known" is an inverted third conditional; the result is would have taken.

items.q: If they ____ the warning, nobody ____ hurt.
items.w: Both halves look back: past perfect, then would have been.

items.q: If I had studied medicine, I ____ a doctor now.
items.w: A past cause with a present result takes past perfect, then would + base verb.

items.q: If she ____ so stubborn, she would have accepted the help.
items.w: A lasting trait behind a past result keeps the second-conditional "were not".

items.q: I ____ the train if I were not always so late.
items.w: A present habit explaining a past event takes would not have missed.

items.q: If he had taken the job, he ____ in Dhaka today.
items.w: The condition is past, the result is now, so the result takes would + base verb.

items.q: Never ____ such a badly argued paper.
items.w: A negative adverb at the front pulls the auxiliary before the subject.

items.q: Not only ____ the deadline, he apologised for it.
items.w: "Not only" at the front of a clause forces did + subject + base verb.

items.q: Rarely ____ a decision reversed so quickly.
items.w: "Rarely" in front position inverts the subject and the auxiliary.

items.q: Only after the audit ____ the scale of the loss.
items.w: "Only after" delays the clause and inverts it: did they understand.

items.q: This route is ____ than the one through the city.
items.w: A one-syllable adjective forms its comparative with -er, not "more".

items.q: The second draft was far ____ than the first.
items.w: A three-syllable adjective takes "more", and "far" only intensifies it.

items.q: The more you practise, ____ it gets.
items.w: The "the more … the more" pattern needs "the" in front of both halves.

items.q: Her handwriting is no ____ than mine.
items.w: "No" before a comparative compares two things: no neater than mine.

items.q: It is ____ building in the district.
items.w: A superlative takes "the": the tallest building.

items.q: That was ____ meal I have ever eaten.
items.w: "Good" is irregular, and the superlative still takes "the": the best.

items.q: This is one of ____ questions on the paper.
items.w: "One of" is followed by a plural noun with a superlative: one of the hardest.

items.q: She is by far ____ candidate we interviewed.
items.w: "By far" intensifies a superlative, which still needs "the".

items.q: I saw ____ cat on the wall. ____ cat was asleep.
items.w: First mention takes "a"; the second mention is known, so it takes "the".

items.q: She plays ____ violin in ____ national orchestra.
items.w: Instruments take "the", and a single named orchestra takes "the".

items.q: ____ honesty is what the job needs most.
items.w: An abstract noun used in general takes no article at all.

items.q: There is not ____ sugar left in the jar.
items.w: "Sugar" is uncountable, so the quantifier is "much".

items.q: ____ of the students had finished, so we waited.
items.w: "Few" without "a" means almost none, which is why they waited.

items.q: We have ____ time — there is no need to run.
items.w: "A little" means some, and it is what makes running unnecessary.

items.q: Could you give me ____ advice?
items.w: "Advice" is uncountable, so it takes "some" and never "an".

items.q: How ____ luggage are you taking?
items.w: "Luggage" is uncountable, so the question word is "how much".

items.q: She gave me two useful ____ of information.
items.w: "Information" cannot be counted directly; you count pieces of it.

items.q: The ____ in this room is unbearable.
items.w: Used generally, "noise" is uncountable and takes no plural or article.

items.q: He has made good ____ this term.
items.w: "Progress" is uncountable, so it takes neither a plural nor "a".

items.q: She avoided ____ the question directly.
items.w: "Avoid" is always followed by the -ing form.

items.q: They agreed ____ the deadline by a week.
items.w: "Agree" takes the to-infinitive.

items.q: On the way home she stopped ____ petrol.
items.w: "Stop to" states the purpose of stopping; "stop -ing" would end a habit.

items.q: Remember ____ the gas before you leave.
items.w: "Remember to" is a future duty; "remember -ing" is a memory.

items.q: Each of the applicants ____ a written test.
items.w: "Each" is singular however plural the phrase after it looks.

items.q: The news ____ better than we expected.
items.w: "News" ends in -s but is singular.

items.q: Either the twins or their mother ____ collecting them.
items.w: With "either … or" the verb agrees with the nearer subject: mother is.

items.q: A number of students ____ still waiting outside.
items.w: "A number of" is plural; only "the number of" takes a singular verb.

items.q: The bridge ____ in 1962.
items.w: The bridge did not act, so the past passive is used: was built.

items.q: The results ____ by the end of the week.
items.w: The future passive is will be + past participle.

items.q: My laptop ____ while I was at lunch.
items.w: The laptop is the thing acted upon, so the verb is passive.

items.q: The proposal is believed ____ by the board already.
items.w: A completed passive after "believed" takes to have been + past participle.

items.q: This form ____ in black ink.
items.w: A modal passive is modal + be + past participle.

items.q: He said he ____ tired.
items.w: Reporting in the past shifts the present back one tense: is becomes was.

items.q: She asked me where I ____.
items.w: A reported question keeps statement word order and drops the auxiliary.

items.q: They told us ____ during the recording.
items.w: A reported instruction takes told + object + (not) to + base verb.

items.q: He said he ____ finish it the following day.
items.w: In reported speech "will" becomes "would".

items.q: She admitted ____ the message.
items.w: "Admit" is followed by the -ing form.

items.q: The woman ____ car was towed is at the desk.
items.w: Possession inside a relative clause takes "whose".

items.q: My sister, ____ lives in Sylhet, is visiting.
items.w: A non-defining clause about a person takes "who", never "that".

items.q: The report ____ we discussed has been withdrawn.
items.w: "What" cannot introduce a relative clause; the thing is picked up by "which".

items.q: The village in ____ she grew up has since flooded.
items.w: After a preposition the relative pronoun must be "which" or "whom".

items.q: Everything ____ could go wrong did.
items.w: After "everything" the relative pronoun is "that", not "what".

items.q: She ____ late for the meeting.
items.w: An adverb of frequency goes after "be": she is never late.

items.q: I ____ finished the first chapter.
items.w: "Already" sits between the auxiliary and the main verb.

items.q: He speaks ____.
items.w: The object comes before the manner adverb: speaks English fluently.

items.q: Could you tell me ____?
items.w: An indirect question keeps statement order: where the office is.

items.q: She bought a ____ table.
items.w: English orders adjectives size, then shape, then material.

items.q: They live in a ____ house.
items.w: Opinion comes first, then age, then material: lovely old brick.

items.q: He wore a ____ jacket.
items.w: Length, then colour, then material: long black leather.

items.q: A ____ vase stood on the shelf.
items.w: Size, then colour, then origin: tall blue Chinese.

items.q: You have met her before, ____?
items.w: A positive statement takes a negative tag repeating the same auxiliary.

items.q: She is not coming, ____?
items.w: A negative statement takes a positive tag.

items.q: Let us start, ____?
items.w: A "let us" suggestion always takes the tag "shall we".

items.q: Nobody phoned, ____?
items.w: "Nobody" is negative, so the tag is positive, and it takes "they".

items.q: Pass me the file, ____?
items.w: A request in the imperative takes the tag "will you".

items.q: I ____ swim every morning before work.
items.w: A past habit that has stopped takes "used to" with a d.

items.q: Did you ____ live in Khulna?
items.w: After "did", "used to" loses its d: did you use to live.

items.q: I am not ____ working nights yet.
items.w: "Be used to" means accustomed to, and is followed by -ing.

items.q: Every summer we ____ walk to the lake after dinner.
items.w: "Would" narrates a repeated past action, though not a past state.

items.q: She ____ have long hair when she was at school.
items.w: A past state takes "used to"; "would" works only for repeated actions.

items.q: I wish I ____ more sleep last night.
items.w: A regret about the past takes wish + past perfect.

items.q: I wish it ____ so humid here.
items.w: A wish about now takes the past form, and "were" for every subject.

items.q: I wish you ____ interrupting me.
items.w: "Wish + would" complains about someone else’s current behaviour.

items.q: If only she ____ us before signing.
items.w: "If only" about the past takes the past perfect, like "wish".

items.q: He regrets ____ the offer.
items.w: "Regret + -ing" is about something already done.

items.q: It was ____ a long queue that we gave up.
items.w: "Such" goes before a noun phrase; "so" goes before a bare adjective.

items.q: The room was ____ small for all of us.
items.w: "Too" means more than is acceptable, which is why it did not work.

items.q: She is not old ____ to vote.
items.w: "Enough" follows the adjective it limits: old enough.

items.q: There were ____ many applicants that we extended the shortlist.
items.w: Before "many" the intensifier is "so", not "such".

items.q: He spoke ____ quietly for anyone at the back to hear.
items.w: "Too … for … to" says the degree defeated the purpose.

items.q: It rained all day; ____, the match went ahead.
items.w: "However" marks a contrast with what came before.

items.q: ____ the delay, the crew finished on schedule.
items.w: "Despite" is followed by a noun; "although" needs a full clause.

items.q: ____ the road was closed, we took the ferry.
items.w: "Since", meaning because, introduces a clause with a subject and a verb.

items.q: The figures were wrong; ____, the whole forecast collapsed.
items.w: "Consequently" introduces the result of what came before.

items.q: Print the ticket, ____ you will not be let in.
items.w: "Otherwise" states what follows if the instruction is ignored.

items.q: The meeting was ____ until Thursday.
items.w: "Put off" means to postpone.

items.q: I cannot ____ this noise any longer.
items.w: "Put up with" means to tolerate.

items.q: Sales ____ sharply after the price rise.
items.w: "Drop off" means to decline; "take off" would mean the opposite.

items.q: The deal ____ at the last minute.
items.w: "Fall through" means to collapse before completion.

items.q: She ____ smoking three years ago.
items.w: "Give up" means to stop doing something.

items.q: We need to ____ the figures before the audit.
items.w: "Go over" means to examine carefully.

items.q: ____ the report, she noticed two errors.
items.w: An action finished before the main one takes "having" + past participle.

items.q: ____ in 1890, the building is now protected.
items.w: A passive participle clause uses the past participle alone: built in 1890.

items.q: ____ the door, he realised he had left the keys inside.
items.w: Two actions at nearly the same moment take the -ing participle.

items.q: Not ____ the language, she relied on gestures.
items.w: A negative participle clause is "not" followed by the -ing form.

items.q: ____ by the noise, the birds scattered.
items.w: The birds received the action, so the participle is passive: startled.
